summary: Kole Jain walks through nine website section layouts he calls trending in 2024. For most of them he shows real websites (or Dribbble shots) that use it, then his Figma wireframe and a finished design; the ninth has no live example. The sections are: cards on a dark background, a thin cropped photo with profound text, giant headline text over a huge image, a scrollable multi-image layout, stacked cards that slide up on scroll, a horizontal card carousel, a bento grid, an image with cut-out lettering, and a text-only section with lots of white space. Each section comes with practical notes: keep spacing precise, put a gradient under text on photos, crop and pick images carefully, match the layout to how much content you have, and give text-only sections enough body copy. For a design system, this is a catalogue of landing-page section patterns, with notes on when each fits, that could be offered to people as visual options.
key_ideas: Cards sitting on a dark background work as a header and can carry a whole website's theme, but the cards must sit very close together with precise spacing.
A thin, cropped photo with really profound text on it works as an interlude or spacer between text-heavy sections.
Text placed on a photo needs a gradient under it, or it is hard to read.
A giant-text hero gets its impact from the contrast between huge headline text and very small navbar text, and placing the navbar beneath the headline makes the headline feel more important.
In the giant-text section, what really brings it together is the massive images, slideshow or video beneath the text.

Images that are blown up large should be large, high-resolution photos so they do not look pixelated, and the thin photo band and the multi-image layout need heavy cropping, so check orientation and aspect ratio when choosing images.
A multi-image layout can show one main large image with more to scroll through, and dot indicators help show how many images there are and how far along you are.
Stacked cards that slide up over each other as you scroll suit a list of three to five options that need some detail.
The horizontal card section is simple and useful but is not used on most websites.
A horizontal card carousel shows a lot of information in a small space; it works for 3 to about 10 cards and should not rely only on small navigation buttons.
Bento grid box sizes change as the content plan develops, and a bento grid needs enough content to fill it.
A cut-out lettering effect over a big image is easy in Figma with subtracts, but the image should not have anything important in the corner the cut-out removes.
A text-only section can open the page up with white space instead of filling the empty area with an image, but it needs three or more lines of body text so it does not feel too empty.

topics.name: Landing pages

topics.name: Cards and sections

rules.rule: When cards sit on top of a dark background, place the rectangles very close to one another and keep the spacing between them precise.
rules.why: The source calls it an important thing to consider for this section; it gives no further reason.
rules.evidence: these rectangles need to come very close to one another

rules.rule: Consider carrying the cards-on-a-dark-background treatment through the whole website, not just the header.
rules.why: Huddle and TOA use it throughout their sites; the source calls it very versatile and easy to work with.
rules.evidence: use this theme throughout the entirety of their website

rules.rule: Put a gradient under text that sits on a photo.
rules.why: Without it the text is pretty difficult to see, which is why the source adds it.
rules.evidence: the gradient that sits under the text

rules.rule: When you have something really profound to say, use a thin, cropped photo with that text on it, as an interlude between two text-heavy sections.
rules.why: A very thin photo acts as a spacer between sections that might be very text heavy.
rules.evidence: an interlude or a spacer between two other sections

rules.rule: Pick images for thin photo bands and multi-image layouts with their crop, aspect ratio and orientation in mind.
rules.why: These layouts need images cropped a lot to fit, so a poorly chosen image will not work.
rules.evidence: we actually need to crop this image a lot in order to get a good aspect ratio

rules.rule: In a giant-text hero, make the headline massive and the navbar text very small, and place the navbar beneath the headline.
rules.why: The size discrepancy is what makes the section look good, and the navbar underneath makes the giant text feel very important.
rules.evidence: the discrepancy between the massive text up here and very small navbar text

rules.rule: Use a display font for giant hero text.
rules.why: The source's giant-text section relies on a nice display font set very large.
rules.evidence: using a nice display font in this case I'm using Oswald and it's very large at 290 pixels

rules.rule: Use a large, high-resolution photo when an image is blown up to fill a hero or section.
rules.why: A small image blown up big appears pixelated.
rules.evidence: use a nice large photo since we are blowing it up quite big

rules.rule: Add dot indicators to a scrollable multi-image layout to show how many images there are and how far along the viewer is.
rules.why: They indicate how many images there are and how far along you are; the source suggests them as an improvement to his own design.
rules.evidence: have some circles down here to indicate how many images there are

rules.rule: Use stacked cards that slide up over each other as the page scrolls when you have a list of three to five options to go through in some detail.
rules.why: The effect lays out the steps of a process right in front of the viewer.
rules.evidence: if you have a list of three to five options that you want to go through in some good detail

rules.rule: Do not make small navigation buttons the only way to move through a horizontal card carousel; add a bigger button or make the cards draggable with the mouse.
rules.why: The source's criticism of Ami is that the only way to navigate is by hitting small buttons.
rules.evidence: the only way of navigating through is by hitting these small little buttons

rules.rule: Keep a horizontal card carousel to 3 to about 10 cards; above 10, consider a different format.
rules.why: Anything more than 10 is a bit cumbersome to click through, and different formats might be better.
rules.evidence: you can display anywhere from 3 to about 10 cards

rules.rule: Expect to resize and re-split bento boxes as the content plan takes shape, and let the content decide the layout.
rules.why: Box sizes often change as content is worked out; in the example, the top row became three boxes instead of two because that suited the content.
values: three boxes instead of just two
rules.evidence: often the size of your boxes is going to change

rules.rule: Only use a bento layout when you have enough content, whether text, images or both, to fill every box.
rules.why: A bento layout displays information compactly, so it needs a fair amount of content.
rules.evidence: it requires a fair amount of content to be able to do a Bento layout

rules.rule: For a cut-out lettering effect over an image, choose an image that fits the space and has nothing important in the top corner that the cut-out would remove.
rules.why: Whatever sits in the cut-out area gets cut off.
rules.evidence: an image that doesn't have anything important in the top Corner

rules.rule: In Figma, make a cut-out image text effect with subtract.
rules.why: The source says it is very easy to accomplish this way.
rules.evidence: very easy to accomplish in figma with some subtracts

rules.rule: In a text-only section, leave the unused area empty rather than filling it with an image, so the text speaks for itself.
rules.why: The section is meant to emphasise text and open up the website with more white space.
rules.evidence: we want to let the text speak for itself

rules.rule: Give the body text in a text-only section three or more lines.
rules.why: Without the extra text the section is too spacious, with too much white space.
rules.evidence: it generally looks better if you have three or more lines to display

rules.rule: In a giant-text hero, put massive images, a slideshow or a video beneath the giant text.
rules.why: The source says the images, or a slideshow displaying massive images, are what really bring the section together.
rules.evidence: what really brings it together is the images or a slideshow

rules.rule: Use a multi-image layout, one main large image with more to scroll through, when you need to show several images plus a bit of text.
rules.why: The source calls it a fantastic way to display multiple images as well as getting a bit of text in.
rules.evidence: a fantastic way to display multiple images

rules.rule: Use a horizontal card carousel to show a large amount of information in a fairly small section.
rules.why: The source calls it a really good section for that, and simple.
rules.evidence: displaying a large amount of information in a fairly small section

rules.rule: After several photo-heavy sections, add a text-only section with the photos taken out to emphasise the text.
rules.why: The source's sections so far had been photo heavy, and he wanted to emphasise the text and open up the website with more white space.
rules.evidence: so far our sections have been pretty photo heavy

decisions.question: Which layout should this website section use?

options.name: Cards on a dark background
options.effect: Rounded rectangles sit tightly together on a dark background; works as a header and as a site-wide theme.
options.when: A header or a consistent look across the whole site, when you can keep spacing very precise.

options.name: Thin cropped photo with profound text
options.effect: A very thin cropped photo with really profound text on it and a gradient under the text; acts as a spacer between sections.
options.when: You have something really profound to say, or need a spacer between two text-heavy sections.

options.name: Giant text over a giant image
options.effect: Massive display headline, small nav links beneath it, then a giant image, slideshow or video; the headline feels very important.
options.when: You want the giant-text trend and have large, high-resolution photos, a slideshow or a video to blow up.

options.name: Multi-image scroll layout
options.effect: One main large image plus more you scroll through with an arrow, with a bit of text; can grow each image as it scrolls past.
options.when: You want to show multiple images and some text together.

options.name: Stacked scroll cards
options.effect: Each card slides up over the previous one as you scroll, laying out steps of a process in front of the viewer.
options.when: A list of three to five options or steps that need some detail.

options.name: Horizontal card carousel
options.effect: A row of cards the viewer moves through with buttons; shows a lot of information in a small space.
options.when: 3 to about 10 cards; more than 10 is cumbersome.

options.name: Bento grid
options.effect: A compact grid of boxes of different sizes (Linear-style), full width or compact.
options.when: You have a fair amount of text and image content to fill the boxes.

options.name: Cut-out image text
options.effect: A big image with uppercase letters sitting in a cut-out; trendy on Dribbble.
options.when: You have an image that fits the space with nothing important in the cut-out corner.

options.name: Text-only with white space
options.effect: No photos; text leads and the empty area opens up the page.
options.when: After several photo-heavy sections, when you have three or more lines of body text.

decisions.question: How should text that sits on a photo stay readable?

options.name: Text directly on the photo
options.effect: The text is pretty difficult to see.
options.when: The source does not recommend it.

options.name: Gradient under the text
options.effect: The text becomes readable against the photo.
options.when: Any time text sits on an image, as in the cropped photo section.

decisions.recommendation: Add a gradient under the text; without it the text is pretty difficult to see.
decisions.evidence: the gradient that sits under the text

decisions.question: How should a multi-image section show its images?

options.name: One main large image with more to scroll through
options.effect: A large lead image and an arrow button to scroll through more images.
options.when: The simpler version of the layout.

options.name: Images that grow as you scroll
options.effect: Each image becomes larger as you scroll through before it leaves the page.
options.when: If you want to get fancier.

decisions.evidence: either you'll have one main large image and more that you can scroll through

decisions.question: How should stacked cards be revealed?

options.name: On scroll (Huddle)
options.effect: The next card slides up as you scroll, revealing the content underneath step by step.
options.when: Walking people through the steps of a process.

options.name: On hover (tapaku Maru)
options.effect: You hover to access each card in the stack.
options.when: The source shows it as an alternative without saying when to choose it.

decisions.recommendation: The source's own design takes more inspiration from Huddle's scroll version, and borrows tapaku Maru's detail of text slightly cut off by the next container; no further reason is given.
decisions.evidence: instead of scrolling in order to get this stacked effect you simply have to hover

decisions.question: How should people move through a horizontal card carousel?

options.name: Small navigation buttons only
options.effect: Works, but moving through is limited to hitting small buttons.
options.when: The source says this is what Ami could do better.

options.name: Small navigation buttons plus a big button
options.effect: Two ways to interact: small nav buttons below and a big button that moves to the right.
options.when: The source's own vineyard design.

options.name: Cards draggable with the mouse
options.effect: People can drag the cards directly.
options.when: Suggested as an improvement to Ami's carousel.

decisions.recommendation: Do not rely on small buttons alone: add a bigger button or make the cards draggable with the mouse.
decisions.evidence: have a button here or make these dragable with the mouse

decisions.question: Should a marketing section use a bento grid, and how wide should it be?

options.name: Compact bento (Linear)
options.effect: A tight, compact bento block.
options.when: Linear's approach.

options.name: Full-width bento
options.effect: The bento grid stretches the full width of the page.
options.when: The source's adaptation for the Evolve example.

options.name: No bento
options.effect: A different section layout.
options.when: You do not have a fair amount of content to fill the boxes.

decisions.recommendation: Use bento only with enough content, and let box sizes change to fit the content plan.
decisions.evidence: ours is going to be full width whereas theirs is much more compact

decisions.question: In a text-heavy section, should the empty area hold an image or stay as white space?

options.name: Add an image
options.effect: Fills the unused area.
options.when: The source says an image could go there.

options.name: Leave it as white space
options.effect: The text speaks for itself and the website opens up with more white space.
options.when: After photo-heavy sections, when you have three or more lines of body text.

decisions.recommendation: Leave it empty and let the text speak for itself, with three or more lines of body text so it is not too spacious.
decisions.evidence: we could have put in an image there but instead we want to let the text speak for itself

decisions.question: How many items do you have to show, and which section pattern fits that count?

options.name: Stacked scroll cards
options.effect: Each card slides up over the one before, walking through the items in some detail.
options.when: A list of three to five options that you want to go through in some good detail.

options.name: Horizontal card carousel
options.effect: A row of cards moved through with buttons (or dragging); lots of information in a small space.
options.when: Anywhere from 3 to about 10 cards.

options.name: A different format
options.effect: Avoids a carousel that is cumbersome to click through.
options.when: More than 10 items; the source says different formats might be better but does not name one.

decisions.recommendation: Stacked cards for three to five detailed options; a carousel for 3 to about 10 cards; for more than 10, a different format might be better.
decisions.evidence: anything more than 10 is a bit cumbersome to click through

process.detail: For each section type, find real websites (or Dribbble shots) that use it and note what makes it work.
Build a simple wireframe of the section's structure before designing it.

process.step: Design a finished version for a real use
process.detail: Apply the wireframe to a specific site, such as a wine tour or vineyard site or a site called Evolve.
As the content plan firms up, adjust box sizes and splits; the bento top row became three boxes instead of two.

process.step: Choose and crop images for the layout
process.detail: Pick high-resolution images whose orientation and aspect ratio suit the layout, expecting heavy cropping.
Review the finished design for gaps, such as adding dot indicators to a multi-image layout.

caveats: The video frames these as trends for 2024; trend status is dated and opinion, not tested evidence.
Many site names come from auto-captions and may be misspelled: 'toa', 'one nil', 'rinse f F', 'maa', 'Studio VI', 'cream', 'tapaku Maru' and 'Ami' (the calendar app is likely Amie [inferred]).
Most judgments are personal taste ('one of my favorites', 'doesn't look too bad'); no data or user testing is given.
No exact spacing, radius, color, gradient or animation values are stated, apart from Oswald at 290 pixels.
The ninth section has no live website example, and the Dribbble screenshots were blurry, per the source.
The source says the Figma file is linked in the video description (the fetched description text does not show the link) and asks viewers to subscribe; this is self-promotion.
No media list was available for this source, so the visuals are described from the narration only.
The auto-caption repeats a sentence about navbar placement, and 'Navar' means navbar.
